note.explanation: Stoichiometry uses a balanced chemical equation and mole ratios to calculate amounts of reactants and products. Convert the given amount to moles, use the equation, then convert to the required unit.
examples: For 10 g of CH₄: 10 ÷ 16 = 0.625 mol CH₄.
The equation gives a 1:1 ratio of CH₄ to CO₂, so 0.625 mol CO₂ forms, which is 0.625 × 44 = 27.5 g.
note.checkAnswer: One mole of CH₄ produces one mole of CO₂, so 10 g CH₄ produces 27.5 g CO₂.
note.simple: A balanced equation is like a recipe: its numbers tell you the mole ratios. Convert what you are given into moles, follow the ratio, and convert to the requested amount.
note.checkQuestion: How many grams of CO₂ form from 10 g of CH₄ when oxygen is in excess?
note.title: Stoichiometry: counting particles and calculating amounts
steps: Write and balance the chemical equation.
Convert the given mass to moles using moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation.
Convert the resulting moles into the required mass or number of particles.

mcqs.stem: Q4.1. How many atoms are present in one gram of H₂O?
rationales: Correct: 1 g is 1/18 mol of water molecules, and each molecule contains three atoms, giving about 1.002 × 10²³ atoms.
This is approximately the number of molecules in 18 g of water, not the atoms in 1 g.
This does not account for all three atoms in each water molecule.
This is about twice the correct count and results from an incorrect conversion.

mcqs.stem: Q4.2. Which is the correct formula of calcium phosphide?
rationales: Calcium is Ca²⁺ and phosphide is P³⁻, so CaP is not electrically neutral.
This formula does not balance the +2 and −3 ionic charges.
The subscripts do not give equal total positive and negative charges.
Correct: three Ca²⁺ ions and two P³⁻ ions balance the charges.

mcqs.stem: Q4.3. How many atomic mass units (amu) are there in one gram?
rationales: One gram is not equal to one atomic mass unit.
This is not the conversion between grams and atomic mass units.
Correct: 1 g is approximately 6.022 × 10²³ amu.
This is ten times smaller than the correct conversion.

mcqs.stem: Q4.4. Structural formula of 2-hexene is CH₃ – CH = CH – (CH₂)₂ – CH₃. What will be its empirical formula?
rationales: C₂H₂ can be reduced to CH, so it is not the empirical formula of C₆H₁₂.
CH does not have the same simplest carbon-to-hydrogen ratio as C₆H₁₂.
C₆H₁₂ is the molecular formula, not the simplest whole-number ratio.
Correct: dividing the subscripts in C₆H₁₂ by 6 gives CH₂.

mcqs.stem: Q4.5. How many moles are there in 25 g of H₂SO₄?
rationales: This is greater than 25 ÷ 98, the correct mass-to-mole calculation.
This is not the result of dividing the mass by the molar mass of H₂SO₄.
Correct: molar mass of H₂SO₄ is 98 g mol⁻¹, so 25 ÷ 98 = 0.255 mol.
This does not follow from the molar mass of H₂SO₄.

mcqs.stem: Q4.6. A necklace has 6g of diamonds in it. What are the number of carbon atoms in it?
rationales: This is about twice the number of atoms in 6 g of carbon.
This is about four times the number of atoms in 6 g of carbon.
This is too small; 6 g of carbon is half a mole of carbon atoms.
Correct: 6 g carbon is 0.5 mol, or about 3.01 × 10²³ carbon atoms.

mcqs.stem: Q4.7. What is the mass of Al in 204g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
rationales: This is not the aluminium mass fraction in Al₂O₃.
This does not account for both Al atoms in each formula unit.
This is the aluminium mass in one mole of Al₂O₃, not in 204 g.
Correct: 204 g is two moles of Al₂O₃, containing four moles of Al, or 108 g.

mcqs.stem: Q4.8. Which one of the following compounds will have the highest percentage of the mass of nitrogen?
rationales: Urea contains nitrogen, but its nitrogen mass percentage is lower than that in N₂H₄.
Correct: nitrogen makes up 28/32 of the mass of N₂H₄, the greatest proportion listed.
Ammonia has a lower nitrogen mass percentage than N₂H₄.
NH₂OH has a lower nitrogen mass percentage than N₂H₄.

mcqs.stem: Q4.9. When one mole of each of the following compounds is reacted with oxygen, which will produce the maximum amount of CO₂?
rationales: One mole of carbon forms one mole of CO₂.
Diamond is carbon, so one mole of carbon atoms forms one mole of CO₂.
Correct: one mole of ethane contains two moles of carbon atoms and forms two moles of CO₂.
One mole of methane forms one mole of CO₂.

mcqs.stem: Q4.10. What mass of 95% CaCO₃ will be required to neutralize 50 cm³ of 0.5M HCl solution?
rationales: This is much greater than the amount calculated from the acid concentration and volume.
This is the mass of pure CaCO₃ required, without adjusting for 95% purity.
Correct: 0.025 mol HCl needs 0.0125 mol CaCO₃; adjusting its 1.25 g pure mass for 95% purity gives about 1.32 g.
This does not correctly apply the 2:1 HCl-to-CaCO₃ ratio and the 95% purity.

written.text: Write down the chemical formula of barium nitride.

rubric.why: The correct ions must be identified.
The subscripts must balance the ionic charges.
rubric.how: Cross the charge magnitudes to obtain Ba₃N₂.

modelAnswer: Barium ion = Ba²⁺; nitride ion = N³⁻.
Cross the charges to balance them: Ba₃N₂.
Barium nitride = Ba₃N₂.

written.text: Find out the molecular formula of a compound whose empirical formula is CH₂O and its molar mass is 180.

rubric.why: The empirical formula mass is needed to find the multiplier.
The final subscripts must all be multiplied by the same whole number.

modelAnswer: Empirical formula mass of CH₂O = 12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30.
n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass = 180 ÷ 30 = 6.
Molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆.

written.text: How many molecules are present in 1.5 g H₂O?

rubric.why: The mass must first be converted to moles.
Avogadro's number converts moles into molecules.

modelAnswer: Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of H₂O = 1.5 ÷ 18 = 0.0833 mol.
Number of molecules = 0.0833 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 5.02 × 10²² molecules.

written.text: What is the difference between a mole and Avogadro's number?
written.finalAnswer: A mole is the amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles; Avogadro's number is the number 6.022 × 10²³.

rubric.why: A mole is a unit for amount of substance.
rubric.how: State that one mole contains a specified number of particles.

rubric.why: The number itself must be distinguished from the unit.

modelAnswer: A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
Avogadro's number is the number 6.022 × 10²³, which gives the number of particles in one mole.

written.text:
Write down the chemical equation of the following reaction.
ANSWER: Copper + Sulphuric acid → Copper sulphate + Sulphur dioxide + Water

rubric.why: All reactants and products must be written with correct formulas.
rubric.description: Writes correct formulas for the substances.
rubric.how: Translate each name into its chemical formula.

rubric.why: A chemical equation must be balanced.
rubric.how: Place coefficients to balance atoms on both sides.

modelAnswer: Cu + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + H₂O
Balance H and O: Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O.

written.text: Different compounds will never have the same molecule formula but they can have the same empirical formula. Explain
written.finalAnswer: Different compounds can have the same simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, but their actual numbers of atoms per molecule can differ.

rubric.why: An empirical formula gives the simplest ratio.
rubric.description: Explains what an empirical formula represents.
rubric.how: State that it is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

rubric.why: A molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in a molecule.
rubric.how: Explain that molecular formulas show actual atom counts.

rubric.why: An example makes the shared empirical formula clear.
rubric.how: Use compounds such as glucose and other compounds sharing an empirical formula.

rubric.why: The explanation must directly address the statement.
rubric.description: Concludes why empirical formulas may match.
rubric.how: Relate the shared simplest ratio to different actual molecular formulas.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule.
Different molecular formulas can reduce to the same simplest ratio; for example, C₆H₁₂O₆ reduces to CH₂O.
Therefore, different compounds can have the same empirical formula but different molecular formulas.

written.text: Write down the chemical formulas of the following compounds. Calcium phosphate, Aluminium nitride, Sodium acetate, Ammonium carbonate and Bismuth sulphate.

rubric.why: Correct ion charges determine these formulas.
rubric.description: Writes calcium phosphate and aluminium nitride formulas.
rubric.how: Balance the charges of each cation and anion.

rubric.why: The acetate ion and sodium ion must be combined in a neutral formula.
Two ammonium ions are required for one carbonate ion.
The final compound must have balanced charges.

modelAnswer: Calcium phosphate = Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
Aluminium nitride = AlN.
Sodium acetate = CH₃COONa.
Ammonium carbonate = (NH₄)₂CO₃.
Bismuth sulphate = Bi₂(SO₄)₃.

written.text: Why does Avogadro's number have an immense importance in chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: It connects the number of atoms, molecules or ions to measurable amounts of substance and makes particle counting possible by weighing.

rubric.why: The numerical value identifies Avogadro's number.
It defines how many particles are in a mole.
rubric.description: Links the number to the mole.
rubric.how: State that one mole contains this number of particles.

rubric.why: Chemistry deals with extremely small particles.
The mole connects microscopic particles to measurable laboratory quantities.
rubric.how: Explain that particles can be counted indirectly by measuring mass.

modelAnswer: Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole.
It tells the number of atoms, molecules or ions present in a mole.
Atoms and molecules are too small to count individually.
The mole and Avogadro's number let chemists relate a measurable mass to the number of particles.

written.text: When 8.657g of a compound were converted into elements, it gave 5.217g of carbon, 0.962g of hydrogen and 2.478g of oxygen. Calculate the percentage of each element present in this compound.

rubric.why: Each percentage uses the total sample mass as the denominator.
rubric.how: Divide the carbon mass by 8.657 g and multiply by 100.

rubric.why: The hydrogen percentage must use its measured mass.
rubric.how: Divide 0.962 g by 8.657 g and multiply by 100.

rubric.why: The oxygen percentage must use its measured mass.
rubric.how: Divide 2.478 g by 8.657 g and multiply by 100.

rubric.why: The percentages should account for the whole sample.
rubric.how: Show that the three percentages sum to about 100%.

rubric.why: The final results must identify all three elements correctly.
rubric.how: Label each calculated percentage with its element.

modelAnswer: Percentage of carbon = (5.217 ÷ 8.657) × 100 = 60.26%.
Percentage of hydrogen = (0.962 ÷ 8.657) × 100 = 11.11%.
Percentage of oxygen = (2.478 ÷ 8.657) × 100 = 28.63%.
Carbon = 60.26%; hydrogen = 11.11%; oxygen = 28.63%.

written.text: How can you calculate the masses of the products formed in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Use the balanced chemical equation and mole ratios to calculate product amounts, taking account of the amount of reactants that actually react.

rubric.why: The balanced equation provides the correct stoichiometric ratios.
Chemical equation coefficients compare amounts in moles.
rubric.how: Convert known quantities to moles and apply the coefficients.

rubric.why: In a reversible reaction, not all reactants necessarily become products.
rubric.description: Accounts for the reaction amount or equilibrium.
rubric.how: Use the amount that actually reacts or the equilibrium composition if supplied.

rubric.why: The result must be expressed as product mass.
rubric.how: Multiply product moles by molar mass.

modelAnswer: Write and balance the chemical equation.
Convert the known reactant quantities into moles.
Use the mole ratio in the balanced equation to find the moles of products formed.
For a reversible reaction, use the amount that actually reacts or the equilibrium amount when given.
Multiply product moles by their molar masses to calculate the product masses.

written.text: Which conditions must be fulfilled before writing a chemical equation for a reaction?
written.finalAnswer: The reactants and products must be identified and written with correct chemical formulas, and the equation must be balanced.

rubric.why: The substances taking part in the reaction must be known.
rubric.how: State that reactants and products must be determined.

rubric.why: A chemical equation uses symbols and formulas.
rubric.how: Write correct symbols and formulas for all substances.

rubric.why: Atoms are conserved in a chemical reaction.
rubric.how: Balance the number of each kind of atom on both sides.

rubric.why: State symbols or reaction conditions may be needed for a complete equation.
rubric.description: Includes relevant state symbols or conditions.
rubric.how: Add state symbols and required conditions when known.

modelAnswer: The reactants and products of the reaction must be identified.
The correct chemical symbols and formulas of all substances must be written.
The equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
State symbols and reaction conditions should be shown when required.

written.text: Explain the concepts of Avogadro's number and mole.
written.finalAnswer: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; this number is Avogadro's number.

rubric.why: The standard number of particles per mole is essential.
A mole counts specified particles.
rubric.how: Mention atoms, molecules, ions or other specified particles.

rubric.why: A mole is an amount-of-substance unit.
rubric.how: Explain that it is a unit for amount of substance.

rubric.why: The concept makes particle counting useful in laboratory work.
rubric.how: Relate amount of substance to measurable mass.

modelAnswer: A mole is a unit for measuring the amount of substance.
One mole of a substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
The number 6.022 × 10²³ is called Avogadro's number.
The particles may be atoms, molecules or ions, and the mole relates their number to a measurable mass.

written.text:
How many grams of CO₂ will be produced when we react 10 g of CH₄ with excess of O₂ according to the following equation?

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)

rubric.why: The given mass must be converted to moles.
rubric.description: Finds the molar mass and moles of methane.

rubric.why: The equation gives the mole ratio between methane and carbon dioxide.
The molar mass of carbon dioxide converts its moles to mass.
The correct product mass follows from moles times molar mass.
The result must be stated with the requested unit.

modelAnswer: Given: mass of CH₄ = 10 g; oxygen is in excess.
Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + 4(1) = 16 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of CH₄ = 10 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.625 mol.
From the equation, CH₄ : CO₂ = 1 : 1, so moles of CO₂ = 0.625 mol.
Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of CO₂ = 0.625 mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 27.5 g CO₂.

written.text:
How many moles of coal are needed to produce 10 moles of CO according to the following equation?

3C(s) + O₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂(g) + 3CO(g)

rubric.why: The balanced equation provides the required coefficients.
rubric.description: Identifies the carbon and CO coefficients.

rubric.why: The coefficient ratio determines the required reactant amount.
rubric.how: Reduce 3 mol C : 3 mol CO to 1 : 1.

rubric.why: The required product amount must be used in the ratio.
rubric.how: Apply the 1:1 ratio to 10 mol CO.

rubric.why: The calculated substance must be identified.
rubric.how: State the moles of carbon needed.

rubric.why: The final answer must have the correct value and unit.

modelAnswer: From the equation, 3 mol C produce 3 mol CO.
Mole ratio C : CO = 3 : 3 = 1 : 1.
Moles of coal (carbon) needed = 10 mol CO × (3 mol C ÷ 3 mol CO).
Moles of coal needed = 10 mol.
Answer: 10 moles of coal (carbon).

written.text:
How much SO₂ is needed in grams to produce 10 moles of sulphur?

2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 3S(s)

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the SO₂-to-sulphur mole ratio.
rubric.how: Use 1 mol SO₂ for every 3 mol S.

rubric.why: The required sulphur amount must be converted to SO₂ moles.
The SO₂ molar mass is needed to obtain grams.
Multiplying moles by molar mass gives mass.
The result must be given in grams as asked.

modelAnswer: From the equation, 1 mol SO₂ produces 3 mol S.
Moles of SO₂ needed = 10 mol S × (1 mol SO₂ ÷ 3 mol S) = 10/3 mol.
Molar mass of SO₂ = 32 + 2(16) = 64 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of SO₂ = (10/3 mol) × 64 g mol⁻¹ = 213.3 g.
Answer: 213.3 g SO₂.

written.text:
How much ammonia is needed in grams to produce 1 kg of urea fertilizer?

2NH₃(aq) + CO₂(aq) → CO(NH₂)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)

rubric.why: The given urea mass must be expressed in grams.
rubric.description: Converts the urea amount to grams.

rubric.why: The urea molar mass converts its mass into moles.
rubric.description: Finds the urea molar mass and amount.

rubric.why: Stoichiometry requires the urea amount in moles.
The equation requires two moles of ammonia per mole of urea.
rubric.how: Double the urea moles to find NH₃ moles.

rubric.why: The final ammonia amount must be converted to mass and labelled.
rubric.how: Multiply NH₃ moles by 17 g mol⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Given: mass of urea = 1 kg = 1000 g.
Molar mass of CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14) + 4(1) = 60 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of urea = 1000 g ÷ 60 g mol⁻¹ = 16.667 mol.
From the equation, NH₃ : urea = 2 : 1.
Moles of NH₃ needed = 2 × 16.667 = 33.333 mol.
Molar mass of NH₃ = 14 + 3(1) = 17 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of NH₃ = 33.333 mol × 17 g mol⁻¹ = 566.7 g NH₃.

written.text:
Calculate the number of atoms in the following.

(a) 3g of H₂

rubric.why: The mass of hydrogen must be converted to moles of H₂ molecules.
rubric.description: Finds the H₂ molar mass and amount.
rubric.how: Use 2 g mol⁻¹ and divide 3 g by 2 g mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: The calculated molecular amount is needed before counting atoms.
Each H₂ molecule contains two atoms.
Avogadro's number converts atom moles into atoms.
rubric.how: Multiply 3 mol of H atoms by 6.022 × 10²³.

rubric.why: The final answer must be the number of atoms.

modelAnswer: Molar mass of H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of H₂ = 3 g ÷ 2 g mol⁻¹ = 1.5 mol.
Each H₂ molecule has 2 H atoms, so moles of H atoms = 1.5 × 2 = 3 mol.
Number of H atoms = 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.806 × 10²⁴ atoms.

written.text:
Calculate the number of atoms in the following.

(b) 3.4 moles of N₂

rubric.why: The given amount is in moles of nitrogen molecules.
Each N₂ molecule contains two nitrogen atoms.
The amount of nitrogen atoms is required before counting them.
Avogadro's number converts atom moles into atoms.
The final result must be expressed as an atom count.

modelAnswer: Each N₂ molecule contains 2 nitrogen atoms.
Moles of N atoms = 3.4 mol N₂ × 2 = 6.8 mol atoms.
Number of atoms = 6.8 × 6.022 × 10²³.
Number of atoms = 4.095 × 10²⁴ atoms.

written.text:
Calculate the number of atoms in the following.

(c) 10g of C₆H₁₂O₆.

rubric.why: The molar mass of glucose is required to convert its mass to moles.
The amount of glucose molecules must be calculated first.
Each glucose molecule contains 24 atoms in total.
rubric.description: Counts the atoms in one glucose molecule.

rubric.why: The total atom amount is needed before applying Avogadro's number.
The requested final quantity is the number of atoms.
rubric.how: Multiply atom moles by Avogadro's number.

modelAnswer: Molar mass of C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of glucose = 10 g ÷ 180 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0556 mol.
Each glucose molecule contains 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms.
Moles of atoms = 0.0556 × 24 = 1.333 mol.
Number of atoms = 1.333 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 8.03 × 10²³ atoms.

written.text: It is generally believed that drinking eight glasses of water every day is required to keep oneself hydrated especially in the summer. If a glass occupies 400 cm³ of water on the average, how many moles of water are needed for a single adult?

rubric.why: The total volume is needed from the number and size of glasses.
The water volume must be converted to mass.
Molar mass converts water mass to moles.
rubric.description: Uses the molar mass of water.

rubric.why: The mole amount must be calculated from mass and molar mass.
The result must state the requested amount and unit.

modelAnswer: Total volume of water = 8 × 400 cm³ = 3200 cm³.
Using density of water = 1 g cm⁻³, mass of water = 3200 g.
Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of water = 3200 g ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 177.8 mol.
Answer: approximately 177.8 moles of water.

written.text: The chemical formula for sand is SiO₂ but the sand does not exist in the form of discrete molecules like H₂O. How has its formula been determined keeping in view its structure?
written.finalAnswer: SiO₂ is the simplest whole-number ratio of silicon to oxygen atoms in the extended crystal structure of sand.

rubric.why: Sand's structure is an extended network rather than separate molecules.
rubric.how: State that silicon dioxide forms a continuous structure.

rubric.why: The formula describes the relative amounts of its elements.
rubric.how: Refer to silicon and oxygen atoms.

rubric.why: The atom ratio is the basis of the formula.
rubric.how: Give one silicon atom for every two oxygen atoms.

rubric.why: The final formula must show the simplest atom ratio.
rubric.how: Write SiO₂ as the empirical or formula-unit ratio.

modelAnswer: Sand has an extended crystal structure and does not consist of separate SiO₂ molecules.
Its formula represents the simplest ratio of the atoms in the structure.
The ratio of silicon atoms to oxygen atoms is 1 : 2.
Therefore, the formula unit is SiO₂.

examTips: Board questions commonly ask you to write ionic formulas, balance equations, calculate empirical or molecular formulas, and explain the mole and Avogadro's number.
For numerical stoichiometry, show the balanced equation, molar mass, conversion to moles, mole ratio, and conversion to the requested unit; these steps earn method marks.
For percentage composition, show each element's mass divided by the total sample mass, multiplied by 100, and check that the percentages add to about 100%.
For atom-counting questions, state whether you are counting molecules or atoms; multiply by the number of atoms in each molecule before using Avogadro's number where needed.
Write units at each stage and include the unit in the final answer.

steps.why: The balanced equation gives the mole relationship between methane and carbon dioxide.
steps.text: Given: mass of CH₄ = 10 g; oxygen is in excess. Equation: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g).

steps.why: A mass must be converted to moles before using the equation's coefficients.
steps.text: Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + 4(1) = 16 g mol⁻¹.

steps.why: Dividing the given mass by the molar mass finds the amount of methane.

explain.title: Formula writing and balancing
explain.body: Write the correct formula for every reactant and product, then balance the equation with coefficients. Do not change the subscripts in a formula when balancing.

explain.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
explain.body: A mole is an amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole.

explain.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
explain.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule and is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

explain.title: Mass and percentage composition
explain.body: Use molar mass to convert between mass and moles. To calculate an element's percentage by mass, divide its mass by the total sample mass and multiply by 100.

explain.title: Stoichiometric calculations
explain.body: A balanced equation gives mole ratios. Convert the given quantity to moles, use the ratio, and then convert the answer to the requested mass or number of particles.

mistakes: Changing formula subscripts instead of adding coefficients when balancing an equation.
Using an unbalanced equation to obtain a mole ratio.
Forgetting to convert grams into moles before using the equation coefficients.
Counting molecules when the question asks for atoms; multiply by the atoms in each molecule.
Confusing the mole, which is an amount of substance, with Avogadro's number, which is a number of particles.
Leaving out units or failing to label which element or substance a final value belongs to.
